opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think AlphaGo was very much in the line of TD-Gammon. If you go back to Gerry Tesauro's work in the early nineties, he had a neural network learning a value function by temporal-difference learning, playing games against itself, and it got to the level of the best human backgammon players. That was a remarkable thing at the time, and in many ways it was the first big success story for reinforcement learning.

AlphaGo is a scaled-up version of that same basic idea. You have a network that learns to evaluate positions, you get it to improve through self-play, and you combine it with search. The search piece, Monte Carlo tree search, was a significant addition, and of course the scale of computation was enormously larger. Go is a much harder game than backgammon in some respects, because there's no dice to smooth things out and the branching factor is huge. So it was a real achievement, and I don't want to take anything away from it.

But conceptually, I wouldn't call it a fundamental departure. It's the same recipe: learn a value function from experience, use self-play to generate that experience, and let computation do the work. What AlphaGo really demonstrated is how far that recipe goes when you give it enough compute. That's sort of the bitter lesson in action. The general methods that scale with computation keep winning out over approaches that try to build in human knowledge.

And then AlphaZero was even more telling, I think, because they stripped out the human game data entirely. It learned purely from self-play, and it was better for it. To me that's the more interesting result. It says that learning from your own experience, rather than imitating people, is the more powerful path. That's something TD-Gammon hinted at decades earlier, and AlphaZero confirmed it in a very dramatic way.

r001.rationale: It calls AlphaGo a “scaled-up version” of TD-Gammon’s basic approach and describes their shared use of value learning and self-play.

r002.rationale: It identifies Monte Carlo tree search as a significant addition to AlphaGo’s approach.

r003.rationale: It does not say AlphaGo learned from final game outcomes instead of temporal-difference learning; it describes the shared approach as value learning from experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to be fair to both. Gerry Tesauro's TD-Gammon in the early nineties already had the essential ingredients: a neural network as the value function, temporal-difference learning, and self-play to generate the experience. It learned to play backgammon at the level of the best humans, with essentially no human knowledge about the game beyond the rules. So in terms of the core idea, AlphaGo was not a departure. It was the same recipe, scaled up.

Now, scaling up is not nothing. Go is a much harder problem than backgammon. The branching factor is enormous, there's no dice to smooth things out, and the position evaluation is notoriously difficult. AlphaGo combined the learned value and policy networks with Monte Carlo tree search, and the networks were deep convolutional networks trained with much more computation. Those engineering achievements were real, and the result captured the world's attention in a way TD-Gammon never did.

But I'd say the version that really mattered scientifically was AlphaGo Zero, the one that threw away the human games. The original AlphaGo was bootstrapped from a database of expert human play, and in that sense it was a step backward from Tesauro's work, which used no such thing. When they removed the human data and learned purely from self-play, the system got stronger, not weaker. That's the lesson. Human knowledge, in the long run, tends to get in the way. Methods that scale with computation and learn from experience win out. TD-Gammon showed that in miniature, and AlphaGo Zero confirmed it at a scale no one could ignore.

So the novelty, to me, is less about new ideas and more about a vindication of old ones.

r001.rationale: It calls AlphaGo “the same recipe, scaled up” from TD-Gammon.

r002.rationale: It identifies Monte Carlo tree search as part of AlphaGo and says its engineering achievements were real, presenting search as a contribution beyond the shared recipe.

r003.rationale: It mentions temporal-difference learning for TD-Gammon, but does not state that AlphaGo learned from final game outcomes instead.

astra-6.text:
I think AlphaGo was a tremendous achievement, but I wouldn’t describe it as a fundamentally new approach to reinforcement learning. TD-Gammon had already demonstrated the central idea: you could learn a value function with a neural network, through self-play, and reach a very high level of play.

AlphaGo brought much more computation, much larger networks, and a very effective combination of learning and search. Of course, there were important technical advances in making all those pieces work together. Go was a much more formidable challenge than backgammon in some respects, and overcoming that challenge deserves enormous credit.

But I distinguish the significance of the accomplishment from the novelty of the underlying ideas. The accomplishment was extraordinary. The underlying story was largely a continuation of something we already understood: learning from experience and using computation to search can take you a very long way.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaGo used more computation and larger networks while continuing TD-Gammon’s central idea of learning a value function through self-play, describing it as a continuation of that approach.

r002.rationale: It mentions combining learning and search, but does not identify a specific innovation in AlphaGo’s search method beyond scaling up.

r003.rationale: The response does not say AlphaGo learned from final game outcomes instead of using temporal-difference learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I see AlphaGo as a tremendous achievement, but more as a culmination of ideas than as a fundamentally new approach to reinforcement learning. TD-Gammon had already demonstrated that you could learn a value function with a neural network through self-play and temporal-difference learning, and achieve a very high level of play.

AlphaGo brought that together with much more effective search, policy learning, and the computational resources to make it work on Go. The original system also learned from human games, whereas TD-Gammon learned through self-play without that kind of instruction.

But I wouldn’t want “these ideas existed before” to diminish the accomplishment. Making them work together at that scale, on a problem people thought was so difficult, was a major achievement. The continuity is part of what makes it exciting: reinforcement learning ideas could go much further than we had previously demonstrated.

r001.rationale: It presents AlphaGo as a culmination of ideas already demonstrated by TD-Gammon and says those ideas were made to work together at greater scale.

r002.rationale: It identifies more effective search, alongside policy learning, as a contribution AlphaGo brought beyond TD-Gammon.

r003.rationale: It says TD-Gammon used temporal-difference learning and AlphaGo learned from human games, but does not state that AlphaGo learned from final game outcomes instead of temporal-difference learning.
